toc.title: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • How to break a complex request into steps and review each one
  • How to iterate: give precise feedback, keep what works, change one thing at a time
  • How to adapt your prompt to the task type: analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming
  • When to start over instead of iterating

2Task Decomposition

Running case

Cedarbrook's Quarterly Review

  • The operations manager pastes sales, returns and complaint data and asks: "Write the quarterly review."
  • Claude produces a long, shallow document that mixes facts and guesses
  • The manager restarts with steps: clean the data, find trends, explain causes, draft the review, then check it

A complex request hides several jobs. Decomposition splits it so each step has a clear input, task and check.

Step What you ask Claude What you check
1. Clarify "Restate the goal and list what you still need from me" Goal and scope are right
2. Plan "Propose an outline or approach before writing anything" The plan fits your need
3. Do the parts One section, one analysis or one question at a time Each part against the source data
4. Combine "Assemble the parts into one document in this structure" Consistency between parts
5. Review "Check the draft against these criteria and list gaps" Final check by you
  • Self-review chain: draft, then review against criteria, then refine is the most common pattern. Ask Claude to critique its own draft against a checklist, then fix it.
  • Decomposition gives you review points: errors are caught early and cheaply instead of being buried in a long answer.
  • You can do the whole chain in one conversation, one step per message, or ask for the plan first and approve it.
  • Very hard reasoning inside one step (math, tricky logic) may benefit from extended thinking (Module 6).
Exam tip

For a long, multi-part business deliverable, the best first move is to ask for a plan or split the work into reviewed steps, not to send one huge request and hope.

3Iteration

Your first prompt is a draft of a request. Treat the first answer as a starting point and refine.

Do Don't
Say exactly what to change: "shorter intro, add the return rate, friendlier tone" Say "make it better"
Keep what works: "keep sections 1 and 3 as they are" Re-ask everything and lose good parts
Change one or two things at a time so you see what helped Rewrite the whole prompt each time
Give examples of what you want Describe a style abstractly only
Add the missing context the first answer revealed Repeat the same prompt expecting a different result
Ask Claude to explain its choices or list assumptions Accept unexplained decisions
  • Compare versions: ask for two variants (for example, a formal and a casual one) and choose, or merge the best parts.
  • Edit an earlier message to branch the conversation: the original thread stays, and you get a separate version to compare.
  • Start a new chat when the thread has drifted, gotten very long, or contains wrong assumptions (Module 8). Paste a short summary of what you decided.
  • Stop iterating when the output meets the criteria you set at the start. More rounds add cost without value.

Exam tip

Good iteration feedback is specific, actionable and tied to your criteria. "Cut to 100 words and add the price" beats "improve it".

4Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type

Task type Goal Prompt strategy Feature that helps
Analysis Find patterns, compare, explain Provide the data, define the question and the output; ask for assumptions and the figures used; ask it to show steps Upload files; thinking for hard reasoning; check numbers yourself
Research Gather and synthesize information State the question, scope and time frame; ask for sources; ask for disagreements among sources; verify key claims Web search for quick facts; Research for deep, multi-source reports
Drafting Produce text for a reader Give audience, purpose, tone, length, key facts; ask for a draft; then iterate on edits Projects hold voice guides; styles
Brainstorming Generate options Ask for many options (10 to 20); encourage variety; set criteria to pick later; then ask to develop the best 2 or 3 Chat; ask for a table scoring options
  • Analysis: ask "what assumptions did you make?" and "show the calculation". Claude can slip on arithmetic, so verify critical numbers (Module 4).
  • Research: separate finding from concluding. Ask for sources, then check the originals. For a current fact (a price, a rule), use web search; for a comprehensive report, use Research.
  • Drafting: the first draft is for editing. Specify the voice; ask for an alternative opening; keep your final edit.
  • Brainstorming: quantity first, judgment second. Do not judge too early; later ask Claude to rank by your criteria. Here Claude's imagination is an asset, and errors matter less than in factual tasks.
Exam tip

Match the strategy to the task. Factual and analytic tasks need sources, checks and assumptions. Creative tasks need volume and variety. Using a creative approach for a factual task is the trap.

5Putting It Together

Running case

Cedarbrook's Competitor Brief

  • Marketing wants a brief on how three rivals price kayaks
  • The strategist asks Claude to plan the brief, then uses Research for the market facts, uploads Cedarbrook's price list for analysis, brainstorms five positioning ideas, and drafts the one-page brief
  • After each step they check the numbers and sources before moving on
Step Task type Feature
Plan the brief Decomposition Chat
Gather rival prices Research Research (with web search)
Compare to our prices Analysis File upload
Positioning ideas Brainstorming Chat
Write the brief Drafting Chat, then edit

6Exam Q&A

S1A manager wants a full competitor analysis, a pricing proposal and a slide outline in one go. What is the best approach?

  • ASend one long prompt and accept the result
  • BAsk for the slide outline only and skip the analysis
  • CAsk Claude to plan the work, then complete and review each part in order
  • DWrite everything manually
Show the answer

Answer: C. Decomposing into reviewed steps catches errors early and improves each part.

S2After a first draft, a director says "make it better" and gets a similar draft. What should they do?

  • ARepeat the same message several times in the hope that a different draft appears
  • BSwitch to a different task and come back to this draft much later without changing anything
  • CGive specific feedback: what to shorten, add, or change in tone
  • DDelete the conversation
Show the answer

Answer: C. Specific, actionable feedback gives Claude a direction to improve.

S3Which prompt strategy fits a brainstorming task best?

  • AAsk for many varied options first, then choose with stated criteria
  • BAsk for one perfect idea
  • CAsk only yes-or-no questions
  • DAsk Claude to cite sources for each idea
Show the answer

Answer: A. Quantity and variety come first; evaluation comes after.

S4A team member asks Claude to analyze a sales CSV. Which addition most improves reliability?

  • AAsk for a shorter answer
  • BRemove the data and ask from memory
  • CAsk Claude to list its assumptions and show the figures it used
  • DAsk Claude to write in a confident tone
Show the answer

Answer: C. Listing assumptions and showing the figures used makes the analysis checkable, which is the best protection against a quiet error.

S5A conversation has drifted, contains a wrong assumption from an hour ago, and answers are getting worse. What is a sensible response?

  • ATurn off all features
  • BKeep adding corrections to the same long thread until the earlier mistakes fade away
  • CAsk the same question five times in a row and pick whichever answer you like the best
  • DStart a new chat with a short summary of the decisions so far
Show the answer

Answer: D. A fresh chat with a summary removes the stale assumption (Module 8).

S6Which TWO describe good decomposition of a long report? Select TWO.

  • AAsk for an outline first and approve it
  • BCheck each section against the source before combining them
  • CAvoid giving Claude the source data
  • DRequest the entire report in one reply with no checkpoints
  • ESkip review because Claude will be accurate
Show the answer

Answer: A, B. Planning and per-part checks are the point of decomposition.

S7For which task is a creative, high-volume approach LEAST appropriate?

  • ASlogan options for a spring campaign aimed at first-time campers
  • BIdeas for a company picnic
  • CNaming ideas for a new tent
  • DSummarizing a legal clause for a customer
Show the answer

Answer: D. Factual and legal summaries need accuracy, sources and review, not volume of variety.

S8Why ask Claude to review its draft against criteria before you read it?

  • AIt can catch gaps and inconsistencies early, so your review focuses on the hard issues
  • BIt removes the need for your own final check because the draft has already been reviewed once
  • CIt guarantees that the draft is now fully correct, since Claude has checked its own work
  • DIt makes the draft longer
Show the answer

Answer: A. Self-review is a useful first pass, not a replacement for your own check.

S9A strategist needs a current fact: a rival's published price for one product. Which option fits?

  • AExtended thinking only, without web access
  • BBrainstorming
  • CA quick web search in a normal chat
  • DResearch mode for a long multi-source report
Show the answer

Answer: C. A simple current fact is a light web-search task; Research is for comprehensive reports.

S10What is the best sign that it is time to stop iterating?

  • AThe text is longer than before
  • BTwenty messages have been sent
  • CThe output meets the criteria set at the start
  • DClaude says it is finished
Show the answer

Answer: C. Criteria defined up front tell you when the output is good enough.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Decompose Clarify, plan, do the parts, combine, review
Self-review chain Draft, review against criteria, refine
Feedback Specific, actionable, tied to criteria; keep what works
Branch Edit an earlier message to compare versions
Restart Drifted or very long thread: new chat plus a summary
Analysis Data plus question; list assumptions; verify numbers
Research Scope, sources, cross-check; web search (light) or Research (deep)
Drafting Audience, tone, key facts; first draft is for editing
Brainstorming Quantity and variety first; judge later with criteria
